sections.readable_text:
The correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] also known as the Pearson correlation coefficient, is denoted [MATH: \rho] (the Greek letter "rho") and is defined as
[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X]\cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}.]

sections.normalized_html:
• The correlation coefficient satisfies [MATH: -1\leq \rho \leq 1.]

  • If [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent random variables, then [MATH: \rho = 0.] The reverse implication does not always hold. In other words, [MATH: \rho=0] does not imply that [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent.

  • Unlike the covariance, [MATH: \rho] is a dimensionless quantity. This means we'll get the same answer regardless of the units used to measure [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

  • Also unlike the covariance, [MATH: \rho] tells the strength of the correlation between [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.] We typically have the following rule of thumb:

    • If [MATH: |\rho| \gt 0.7,] the correlation is strong, and the data generated by our two random variables closely follow a straight line.

    • If [MATH: 0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,] the correlation is weak. The data generated by our random variables follow a straight line, but many are far from the line.

    • If [MATH: |\rho| \lt 0.3,] then the correlation is negligible. No (linear) correlation exists between the data points generated by the random variables.

Content:
Let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] be two random variables with covariance [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] and standard deviations [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y].]

Content:
The correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] also known as the Pearson correlation coefficient, is denoted [MATH: \rho] (the Greek letter "rho") and is defined as
[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X]\cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}.]

Content:

[MATH: -1\leq \rho \leq 1.]
- If [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent random variables, then
[MATH: \rho = 0.]
The reverse implication does not always hold. In other words, [MATH: \rho=0] does not imply that [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent.
- Unlike the covariance, [MATH: \rho] is a dimensionless quantity. This means we'll get the same answer regardless of the units used to measure [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

- If [MATH: |\rho| \gt 0.7,] the correlation is strong, and the data generated by our two random variables closely follow a straight line.

sections.readable_text: The variances of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are [MATH: 25] and [MATH: 36,] respectively. Given that [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 18,] find the correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is defined as

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},]

where

  • [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] is the covariance, and

  • [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y]] are the standard deviations of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: SD[X]|= sqrt(Var[X]) = sqrt(25) = 5,; SD[X]|= sqrt(Var[Y]) = sqrt(36) = 6.]

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

[MATH: ρ|= (Cov[X, Y])/(SD[X] ⋅ SD[X]); = (18)/(5 ⋅ 6); = (3)/(5).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is defined as

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},]

The joint probability mass function [MATH: f(x,y)] for the discrete random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is shown above. Given that
[MATH: \textrm {E}[X]=0.4\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]=0.6, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X] \approx 0.4899, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.4899,]
find the correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.] Round your answer to [MATH: 2] decimal places.

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is defined as

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},]

where

  • [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] is the covariance, and

  • [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y]] are the standard deviations of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

[MATH: E[XY]|= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})∑_(y ∈ S_{Y})xyf(x, y); = 0 ⋅ 0 ⋅ 0.1 + 0 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 0.5; = + 1 ⋅ 0 ⋅ 0.3 + 1 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 0.1; = 0.1.]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

[MATH: Cov[X, Y]|= E[XY] − E[X] ⋅ E[Y]; = 0.1 − (0.4)(0.6); = − 0.14.]

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

[MATH: ρ|= (Cov[X, Y])/(SD[X] ⋅ SD[Y]); ≈ (− 0.14)/(0.4899 ⋅ 0.4899); ≈ − 0.58,]

rounded to [MATH: 2] decimal places.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] be two random variables with covariance [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] and standard deviations [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y].]

Content:
The correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y,] also known as the Pearson correlation coefficient, is denoted [MATH: \rho] (the Greek letter "rho") and is defined as
[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X]\cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- The correlation coefficient satisfies
[MATH: -1\leq \rho \leq 1.]
- If [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent random variables, then
[MATH: \rho = 0.]
The reverse implication does not always hold. In other words, [MATH: \rho=0] does not imply that [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are independent.
- Unlike the covariance, [MATH: \rho] is a dimensionless quantity. This means we'll get the same answer regardless of the units used to measure [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]
- Also unlike the covariance, [MATH: \rho] tells the strength of the correlation between [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.] We typically have the following rule of thumb:

- If [MATH: |\rho| \gt 0.7,] the correlation is strong, and the data generated by our two random variables closely follow a straight line.

[IMG: /graphics/f0270db56b4f5649417e8ee6324fd37b]
- If [MATH: 0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,] the correlation is weak. The data generated by our random variables follow a straight line, but many are far from the line.

[IMG: /graphics/7eb82da0f2bdb708e68dbb8ed6c4c61f]
- If [MATH: |\rho| \lt 0.3,] then the correlation is negligible. No (linear) correlation exists between the data points generated by the random variables.

[IMG: /graphics/cfe3ae895a0004fb5edf6dda9b728fec]

Content:
Let's get some practice computing the correlation coefficient.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance

Example Prompt:
The variances of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] are [MATH: 25] and [MATH: 36,] respectively. Given that [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 18,] find the correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is defined as

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},]

where

- [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] is the covariance, and
- [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y]] are the standard deviations of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

In our case, we have

[MATH: SD[X]|= sqrt(Var[X]) = sqrt(25) = 5,; SD[X]|= sqrt(Var[Y]) = sqrt(36) = 6.]

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

[MATH: ρ|= (Cov[X, Y])/(SD[X] ⋅ SD[X]); = (18)/(5 ⋅ 6); = (3)/(5).]

Item 5 — Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables

Example Prompt:
| [MATH: f(x,y)] | [MATH: Y=0] | [MATH: Y=1] | [MATH: f_X] |
| [MATH: X=0] | [MATH: 0.1] | [MATH: 0.5] | [MATH: 0.6] |
| [MATH: X=1] | [MATH: 0.3] | [MATH: 0.1] | [MATH: 0.4] |
| [MATH: f_Y] | [MATH: 0.4] | [MATH: 0.6] | [MATH: 1] |

The joint probability mass function [MATH: f(x,y)] for the discrete random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is shown above. Given that
[MATH: \textrm {E}[X]=0.4\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]=0.6, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X] \approx 0.4899, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.4899,]
find the correlation coefficient of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.] Round your answer to [MATH: 2] decimal places.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y] is defined as

[MATH: \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},]

where

- [MATH: \textrm{Cov}[X, Y]] is the covariance, and
- [MATH: \textrm {SD}[X]] and [MATH: \textrm {SD}[Y]] are the standard deviations of [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.]

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

[MATH: E[XY]|= ∑_(x ∈ S_{X})∑_(y ∈ S_{Y})xyf(x, y); = 0 ⋅ 0 ⋅ 0.1 + 0 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 0.5; = + 1 ⋅ 0 ⋅ 0.3 + 1 ⋅ 1 ⋅ 0.1; = 0.1.]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

[MATH: Cov[X, Y]|= E[XY] − E[X] ⋅ E[Y]; = 0.1 − (0.4)(0.6); = − 0.14.]

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

[MATH: ρ|= (Cov[X, Y])/(SD[X] ⋅ SD[Y]); ≈ (− 0.14)/(0.4899 ⋅ 0.4899); ≈ − 0.58,]

rounded to [MATH: 2] decimal places.
